name: effect size
short: A number showing how large a difference or relationship is (d, r and the like); statistical significance only tells whether it could be chance.
html:
Effect size is the number showing how large a difference or relationship is: Cohen’s d, which expresses a mean difference in standard-deviation units, or r, which expresses a relationship. Statistical significance only answers “could this difference be chance?”, and as the sample grows even very small differences turn out “significant”.

In the 689,003-user Facebook experiment of Kramer and colleagues some comparisons gave p < .001 but Cohen’s d lay between 0.001 and 0.02. The American Statistical Association’s 2016 statement says that a p-value does not measure the size of an effect or the importance of a result. Funder and Ozer suggest reference points for r such as .05 (very small but potentially consequential over time), .10 (small), .20 (medium) and .30 (large). See meta-analysis.
example: A d = 0.01 difference turning out “significant” in an experiment with millions of users while being tiny in practice.
